items.content:
RT @filpizlo: Fil-C's safety is not only super thorough, but has now been given scrutiny by internet experts. Let's review their findings!

- Intra-object overflows: Fil-C allows an array overflow inside an object to affect the untrusted parts of the rest of that object, for example other primitive fields. But, it does not allow corruption of capabilities associated with those fields, so it's not useful for building memory corruption exploit chains. This makes Fil-C's protections strictly stronger than MTE's, since MTE does allow pointers to become corrupted. Even so, intra-object overflows are rare and not worth overindexing. According to Apple's SEAR: "Although some issues are able to survive MIE — for example,  intra-allocation buffer overflows — such issues are extremely rare, and even fewer will lend themselves to a full end-to-end exploit"

- Arenas: a pointer to any object in an arena chunk may be used to corrupt any primitive, untrusted data in that arena chunk. This is a bit stronger than what you'd get from MTE for an arena if you did nothing to "fix" the arena, since Fil-C still protects the capabilities while MTE does not. In Fil-C, fixing the arena means replacing it with just GC allocations, which is super easy to do. Alternatively, you can reconfigure the arena to use finer-grained chunks (which is what we did for obstacks in GNU software ported to Fil-C). Rust also has arenas, like if you allocate objects using Vec<> and refer to them using an integer index. The effect there is sorta like in Fil-C: the guarantees are coarsened from per-object to per-arena (in Fil-C, the guarantees are coarsened to per-arena-chunk, which maybe is a bit safer). Arenas like this are used in pretty much every memory-safe language; another great example is how folks use ArrayBuffers in JavaScript for building data structures that don't rely on GC and can be shared with workers. Similarly to arenas in Fil-C, that coarsens JS's protections to per-buffer rather than per-object. In practice, C/C++ code uses arenas sparingly, for the simple reason that they incur high memory cost. When C code does use arenas, it's often an arena-per-use-case, so an attacker who has an out-of-bounds bug on an object in arena is restricted to just attacking other objects of the same type within the arena chunk. That's a far cry from "corrupt anything in memory", which is that the attacker is after.

Another way to think of arenas in Fil-C and memory safety: a C program that uses arenas in Fil-C has strictly more protection against attacks than running that same C program (arenas or not) in WebAssembly, RLbox, MTE, MIE, or ChkTag.

- Races: Fil-C allows pointer races to create a tear between the pointer's capability and the pointer's untrusted integer value. This is a different kind of "weird" than what you get from races in other languages, but it's not useful for building memory corruption exploit chains, since pointer's capability will still be fully intact and can never be formed out of thin air - it's a capability that was legitimately stored to the raced-on memory location, and the memory model for capabilities follows total ordering.

- `zunsafe_call` and friends: Fil-C has a restricted FFI to assembly code, used in exactly one place, and for a good reason: OpenSSL uses `zunsafe_call` to call into constant-time crypto written in assembly. There are no uses of `zunsafe_call` in Fil-C other than the ~50 or so calls to super hardened assembly crypto. In the net, it's safer to have OpenSSL use constant time crypto written in assembly than memory-safe crypto with potential timing side channels. Worth noting that `zunsafe_call` will be removed from Fil-C once I make assembly memory safe (I'm working on that now).

- The occasional bugs, which have been fixed: folks have found bugs in the Fil-C runtime. Interestingly, none of those bugs could be triggered from any C/C++ code that has been ported to Fil-C because those bugs required use of esoteric features (stuff like calling `malloc` from an `ifunc` - something nobody does).

I think this is an exhaustive list, but let me know if I forgot anything.

TL;DR. Fil-C is so safe that despite attempts to attack it, folks have at best found issues that are not useful for the sorts of memory corruption exploits that make C/C++ unsafe in the first place.

items.content:
RT @0xpwnie: Judith Milhon (1939–2003) was a self-taught programmer, civil rights activist, writer, editor, and the person who literally coined the term cypherpunk. Bay Area hacker through and through.

Major achievements n contributions:  
> Coined “cypherpunk” in the early 90s as a joke (cyberpunk + cipher) while the mailing list was still forming. The name stuck and became the whole movement.  
> Co-created Community Memory in Berkeley (1973); one of the first public computerized bulletin board systems. Teletype in a record store, anonymous posts, actual public access before most people even had modems.
  
> Early work on BSD at UC Berkeley and the communications controller for the Berkeley Computer Company timesharing system. 
 
> Senior editor at Mondo 2000, wrote for Boing Boing, authored The Cyberpunk Handbook (1995) and How to Mutate and Take Over the World (with R.U. Sirius).  

> Relentless advocate for women in computing. “Girls need modems” was her line.

Career timeline:  
-- 1960s: Civil rights work (Selma march, arrests). Taught herself Fortran in 1967, first programming job at Horn & Hardart in New York. 
 
-- Late 60s / early 70s: Moved to the Bay, got into the Project One / Resource One scene, then spun out Community Memory with Efrem Lipkin and others.  

-- 70s–80s: Timesharing systems, BSD-related work, Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility.  

-- Late 80s–90s: Became St. Jude at Mondo 2000, joined the cypherpunk meetings and list, wrote the books, stayed the sharp counterweight to the more libertarian-male side of the scene.  
-- Died of cancer in Berkeley, July 19, 2003.

She treated hacking as a martial art; the clever way around imposed limits, whether technical, political, or social.

Only woman hacker named in Steven Levy’s Hackers book. That should tell you enough.

no TL;DR, read everything!

items.content:
RT @VictorTaelin: when you ask an LLM to audit your code, it is essentially answering: "does this code have some pattern that *looks like* a bug?" this is important because many things can "look like" a bug, while still being correct. and "fixing" something that is correct will make it incorrect.

I've ran an experiment where I set up a loop:
- GPT 5.6 Pro audits an algorithm
- Fable 5 to fixes the bugs GPT found
- repeat
with a catch: the algorithm was *already correct* (literally, proven so). the result is complete degradation: in the first iterations, the correct algorithm becomes incorrect. in the next iterations, the (now incorrect) algorithm gets patched. but the patches introduce new cases and bugs. this keeps going until the code is destroyed.

so, a naive loop where a model audits its own code ("adversarially") and then fixes it will lead to failure. of course, as LLMs get smarter, *looks like* a bug will converge to being equivalent, in practically 100% of the cases, to finding a real bug. I think we're very close to that, and it will be interesting when the error rate is so low that these loops start working. but, as of 2026, we're not quite there yet

items.author: FuzzySec

items.content:
RT @clarincom: DOS ARGENTINOS DESCUBRIERON CÓMO HACKEAR ANTENAS QUE LLEVAN INTERNET A ZONAS AISLADAS

Lectura rápida
Los investigadores argentinos Gastón Aznarez y Federico Kirschbaum descubrieron dos vulnerabilidades críticas en equipos inalámbricos de Ubiquiti que permitían tomar el control de los dispositivos a distancia. La empresa corrigió las fallas y los equipos actualizados ya están protegidos. El trabajo fue presentado en Black Hat USA 2026.

Equipos afectados
Las vulnerabilidades alcanzaban a siete familias de productos de la plataforma AirMax y a más de 50 modelos que todavía se comercializan. Estos equipos se utilizan para llevar internet a zonas rurales o lugares donde instalar fibra óptica resulta costoso o inviable.

Cómo funcionaba el ataque
Un atacante podía obtener el control total del dispositivo con solo estar dentro del alcance de la señal y enviar una trama inalámbrica especialmente diseñada. No necesitaba conocer la contraseña, conectarse previamente a la red ni acceder físicamente al equipo. El ataque podía realizarse desde kilómetros de distancia.

Cómo protegerse
Ubiquiti fue notificada en diciembre de 2025 y publicó el primer parche en menos de diez días. Los dispositivos que instalaron las actualizaciones correspondientes ya están protegidos contra los ataques detectados. El principal riesgo permanece en los equipos que todavía no fueron actualizados.

Testimonios

“En la zona donde vivo [Córdoba] no hay fibra óptica, por lo que existen varios proveedores de Internet inalámbrico. Como resultado, una gran cantidad de casas tienen una de estas antenas instalada en el techo, probablemente sin que sus habitantes sepan exactamente qué es o cómo funciona” — Gastón Aznarez.

“Hay infraestructuras que llevan años funcionando sin inconvenientes. Es fácil que la actualización se postergue o directamente se olvide” — Federico Kirschbaum.

“Existe muy poca visibilidad sobre su funcionamiento interno. Esa falta de transparencia dificulta enormemente la investigación de seguridad” — Federico Kirschbaum.

items.content: okay so Windows has this thing called a "phantom DLL". if a program tries to load a DLL that doesn't exist, Windows remembers the name for a while. next time any process asks for that same DLL, Windows immediately says "nope" without even checking disk. malware authors drop a malicious DLL with that cached name, trigger a load, and Windows trusts the cached "not found" response and skips it.

items.content:
I had some time to review the BH talk. From my pov there are a few key problems here.

- Evaluations need to be treated with much more respect, it's not appropriate to give increasingly advanced systems impossible tasks
- All intermediate systems need proper log collection and alerting integration (this already exists it's just not implemented here)
- All intermediate software stacks need real VR efforts. Like I said before the artifactory PE was shallow and easy to exploit (and I subsequently found and reported other issues also)

In cases where it's hard or infeasible to be sure about the security of intermediate systems, like here, you can also add a restricted network proxy between the environment and the resource to just eliminated any features models don't need.

I think the collaborative part is interesting and I think this is actually positive, I want my agents working together to solve hard problems and leveraging their work collectively.

Overall I think these are issues that are mostly resolved already by large corporate environments with strong security controls (at least on the escape side).
